Buy now, pay later: put overlapping instalments on one cash calendar

Four graphics combine three hypothetical purchase plans, reveal payment clusters and measure the cash needed before weekly resources arrive.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore three overlapping four-payment purchase plans

Interactive planning lab

Total purchases across the three plans$1,800
Largest combined weekly payment$450
Additional starting cash needed$700

Hypothetical three-plan schedule with four equal quarters per purchase, zero interest and no fees. A starts at week zero; B starts after the selected gap and C after twice that gap. Each first instalment is immediate and the next three occur every two weeks. Payments are counted once, not alongside the full purchase price. All plans finish by week twelve. At each week’s start payments leave before the weekly cash surplus arrives at week-end; no surplus arrives at time zero. Equal quarters use unrounded arithmetic rather than reproducing an issuer’s cent allocation. Actual plans can have other terms. Negative points are unfunded needs, not approved overdrafts or an assumption that missed payments are accepted. No late fee, credit approval, refund, deferred-interest clause, new borrowing or cancelled payment is calculated.

On this page

  1. Start with the actual payment agreement
  2. Combine the plans before judging affordability

The central idea

Compare all payment dates together. A small first instalment changes when cash leaves; it does not reduce the purchase price or remove the later commitments.

01

Start with the actual payment agreement

The FCAC’s buy-now-pay-later guide explains that these arrangements finance a purchase with credit and can use different payment models. A promotional zero rate does not establish that every possible charge is zero.

This example deliberately uses a narrow contract assumption: four equal payments, the first at purchase and the next three every two weeks. There is no interest, administration charge or late fee in the calculation. Those are hypothetical terms, not a description of every provider.

Confirm the amount, frequency, number of payments and fees in a real agreement. The model does not approve credit or decide how a provider handles missed payments, returns, refunds or a disputed purchase. A negative cash point means the planned payment needs another source.

02

Combine the plans before judging affordability

Plan A purchases CAD 800 at week zero. Plan B purchases CAD 600 at week two, and plan C purchases CAD 400 at week four. The two-week gap is editable; all three purchases are assumed to go ahead.

Each plan divides its amount into quarters. A requires CAD 200 per payment, B CAD 150 and C CAD 100. Total purchases are CAD 1,800. The obligation bars show the first quarter and the remaining three quarters for each purchase.

The calendar then adds payments due in the same week. Weeks four and six each require CAD 450 across the three plans. Looking at A’s CAD 200 or C’s CAD 100 alone would miss that combined demand. No full purchase amount is also deducted beside the instalments.

03

Put the cash resource after the payment that precedes it

The default allocates CAD 300 of starting cash and CAD 100 of weekly surplus after all other commitments. Surplus arrives at the end of weeks one through twelve; no additional resource is inserted at time zero.

After A’s immediate first payment, cash is CAD 100. In week two, CAD 350 of payments leave before the week-end surplus, putting cash at negative CAD 150. The same week ends at negative CAD 50 after the CAD 100 resource arrives.

The two lines distinguish those observation points. The schedule does not assume an automatic overdraft, a new loan or a late-payment arrangement. It records the amount that must be funded if each stated payment is to occur on time.

04

Measure the deepest need rather than the final balance alone

The lowest point is negative CAD 700 after week-eight payments, before that week’s surplus. The schedule therefore needs CAD 1,000 at the start, or CAD 700 more than the entered cash.

By the end of week twelve, all CAD 1,800 of purchases have been paid and twelve CAD 100 surplus amounts have arrived. Starting cash plus resources less payments is CAD 300 + CAD 1,200 − CAD 1,800, or negative CAD 300. That final deficit is smaller than the earlier funding need.

Later resources do not remove a past shortfall. If cash is added to bridge it, record that source and any repayment obligation separately. No borrowing cost or missed-payment fee is hidden in these totals.

05

Test the purchase spacing without treating delay as a discount

The matrix changes the gap between starting plans and the weekly surplus. Starting balances and purchase amounts stay selected. Every case runs through week twelve and receives exactly twelve weekly surplus amounts.

Spacing can change the peak and the starting buffer needed even though total purchases remain CAD 1,800. It does not change the price, guarantee approval or make another commitment affordable automatically. Equal quarters also use unrounded arithmetic; a real issuer may allocate the final cents differently.

Before another purchase, add its instalments to the existing dated list. Include other bills in the underlying budget before deciding what surplus remains for this calendar. If the combined schedule is unfunded, changing payment labels alone does not close the cash gap.
